newsitem.title: GERMANY: German coal deal a short-term fix - analysts.
newsitem.headline: German coal deal a short-term fix - analysts.

text.p: Chancellor Helmut Kohl eased the pressure on his beleagured government on Thursday by striking a compromise on coal subsidies which placated angry miners without putting an extra burden on state finances this year.
Bonn said a deal on coal aid, as well as the costs of a planned 25 billion mark ($15 billion) offensive to boost building investment, would not cost the federal government a single mark this year.
But independent economists warned that Kohl was trying to buy industrial peace with short-term palliatives which would fail to give the economy a real lift.
And, despite the coal deal and building drive, a further round of fiscal belt-tightening will be needed if Germany is to pass muster for European monetary union (EMU), they said.
"It's not looking great, and time is running out," said Stephen King, European economist at HSBC James Capel in London.

Ruetger Teuscher, economist at Deutsche Bank Research, said Finance Minister Theo Waigel would still have to cut 10 billion marks in spending this year to hit the Maastricht treaty budget deficit target of three percent of GDP. If no action is taken, he said, the deficit will hit 3.3 percent of GDP.
Some analysts said government promises of 500 million marks a year in extra federal coal subsidies starting next year could endanger lasting adherence to the Maastricht criteria.
And the construction drive, to be financed by off-budget development loans, will meet a weak response from a building industry in secular decline after its post-unification boom.
"From the point of view of Maastricht this is fine," King said. "But it does raise the issue of medium-term sustainability."
Kohl's Christian Democrats (CDU) appealed to the opposition Social Democrats (SPD) to return to talks on crucial tax reforms which were suspended during the week-long coal dispute.

But SPD leader Oskar Lafontaine repeated conditions for restarting the talks, saying the government must come up with new proposals to relieve the burden on ordinary workers next year before the talks can resume.
Analysts said, however, that the chances of striking a compromise to avoid trench warfare in parliament -- where the SPD can veto tax changes -- had tumbled.
Gerhard Grebe, at Bank Julius Baer in Frankfurt, said the climate had been "poisoned" by the coal stand-off, and chances for a tax deal had become "significantly worse".

"What I can't understand is why the government fomented this conflict over coal now," Grebe said. He added the problem could have been dealt with later -- and had no impact on state finances this year in any case.
The SPD may have also learned that votes are to be won by taking a popular stand against government austerity measures, King said. General elections are due in autumn 1998.

King added that, while he shared the government's forecast of economic growth of 2.5 percent this year, the upturn was led by exports rather than tax-generating domestic demand. "It's the wrong kind of growth," he said.

That meant that his budget deficit forecast of 3.3 percent of GDP still had upside risks. Grebe forecasts 3.2 percent, but also said a poor showing in tax revenue estimates due in May would prompt him to revise up his deficit forecast.
Views remain split on whether Germany's budget woes will lead European leaders next year to interpret Maastricht generously so that EMU can start on time, or whether they will announce a delay.
Grebe said the Maastricht criteria would be weakened and leaders would count on the stability pact -- a deal to punish fiscal laxity -- to ensure discipline under the new currency.
But King said a postponement was more likely: "It is difficult for Germany to entertain the idea of Italy being in the first wave in 1999."
($ = 1.695 German Marks)
